paragraphs.source_en: The arrangement of stones into a semicircle is clearly artificial as single pieces of stones are put side by side, in the centre of this construction only the stones are accumulated to a height not exceeding 30 cm. The parapet belongs to the prehistoric period as all stones present a black patina, absent in the lower part covered by the soil. Based on the study of the patina (Cremaschi 1998; Mori 2000) it should date at least to 3,400 BP, however, a more ancient age is probable. Semicircle structures excavated in the Tassili at Tin Hanakaten and in the Acacus at Tin Torha and dated to the 10th millennium BP (Barich 1987; Aumassip 1980-1) suggest that the structure at Tin Aboteka may be contemporaneous.

paragraphs.source_en: The semicircle structure does not seem to have had practical reasons such as a wind-break wall or an enclosure for animals. If people wanted to use the shelter for dwelling, they would have gone inside the stone city where there were protected shelters with roofs, much more suitable for living than this exposed wall on a hill, which had to be very windy in winter and hot in summer. The same is true for a probable enclosure for animals; not only is the parapet too low but the painted wall is too short and without any roof so that it appears to be the least convenient place for keeping animals in the whole site. Due to the nature of the paintings, with a strong emphasis of masks as a probable ritual element, I suggest that this stone semicircle in front of the composition belongs to it, possibly to indicate a special-status area.

paragraphs.source_en: The next shelter is dominated by a big indeterminable animal about 2 m in length with a long tail and the head pointing downwards (Fig. 5-2). It is one of the best examples of the so called down-headed animals which is one of the characteristic elements of the Round Head art and is interpreted later. The animal has at least three painted borders–brown, red and white– which are not completely overlapping. Moreover, the head of this quadruped seems to be repainted with a different red ochre than that of the body. Repainting is a frequent phenomenon in the Round Head art and might have at least two explanations. Firstly, an old figure was repainted by a new, presumably more important one. Secondly, there was a unique figure which could have been repainted several times, not always following exactly the previous shape.
